summary: Outpost Command is a game where students design and run a Moon or Mars outpost. Before launch, players split limited rocket weight between solar panels, batteries, radiation shielding, a greenhouse and spare parts. Then they keep three astronauts alive for 14 days through lunar nights, dust storms and solar flares, choosing each day how to spend crew time and power. Every choice costs something, so missions can fail, and a debrief explains exactly why. Players can replay real events, such as Opportunity’s 2018 dust storm, Chandrayaan-3’s lunar night and the 1972 solar storm, and rewind to try a different decision. It makes real engineering trade-offs tangible and fun without overwhelming young learners, using a tutorial, a simple Junior view and 18 languages. NASA data and videos power the learning, and teachers can run it in class with no accounts.
details:
What it does
Outpost Command lets students experience the decisions behind a real mission. First, in “Design your outpost”, players split 10 units of launch weight across five systems: solar panels, batteries, radiation shielding, a greenhouse and spare parts. These limits are physical: battery size sets how much power can be stored, shielding sets the most radiation protection crew work can reach, and spare parts decide how far repairs can restore life support. Then they run the outpost for 14 days with three astronauts, choosing two crew jobs a day and whether to spend power on grow lights and the science lab. Core events (cargo landers, solar storms, leaks, the lunar night, Mars dust storms, illness) and 11 random extra events, such as mold, water ice and a dust devil, force trade-offs where every option costs something. After each day, colored chips show what changed. At the end, a debrief names the main cause of success or failure, explains how the launch design mattered, and shows the real NASA science and NASA videos behind it.

How it addresses the challenge
It covers life support, radiation shielding, power and food production, and lets missions fail or succeed on the player’s decisions. It avoids oversimplifying through real figures (Moon and Mars radiation levels, Mars sunlight at about 43% of Earth’s, lunar night, ISS water recycling). It avoids overwhelming young learners with a 4-step tutorial, a Junior view with six simple bars (Commander mode shows every number), a daily tip from the Cosmo companion, and a “what if?” rewind to any decision day.

What makes it creative
Mission History lets players replay real events: NASA’s Opportunity rover and the 2018 dust storm, India’s Chandrayaan-3 and the lunar night, and the 1972 solar storm between Apollo 16 and 17. They try to survive what history could not, then read what really happened. The storm in a mission can come from the strongest real solar flare in NASA’s DONKI space-weather database. Players earn stars, badges, levels and a companion wardrobe, with no streak pressure.

Benefits and intended impact
Students learn that engineering is about trade-offs, and teachers get tools to prove it. A before-and-after learning check uses different questions on the same ideas and explains every answer. Teacher mode creates class codes, so a whole class plays the same scenario, and a dashboard shows average scores, common causes of failure and learning gain. It needs no accounts and stores no student data on a server. Crew mode lets three students share one phone. The game supports 18 languages with a searchable language screen, color-blind friendly bars, adjustable text size, a reduced-motion option and a kid-safe mode.

Tools
React Native, Expo and TypeScript, with react-native-svg for the planets, Supabase for optional sync and AI functions, Jest and tsx for automated tests, and Netlify and GitHub for the web version and code. NASA resources used: the NASA Image and Video Library, Astronomy Picture of the Day and DONKI APIs. The simulation is a deterministic, tested engine, so every result can be explained. It runs on phones and in a web browser; no special hardware is needed.

Use of Super Intelligence
Code, tests, data tables, text and translations were created with help from Claude (Anthropic) and reviewed by the team. The sound effects are generated by a script, and the visuals are drawn in code. The game contains no NASA logos or mission identifiers.

Factors considered and limits
We simplified the numbers into a 0 to 100 scale and shortened the lunar night in one replay, so it is a teaching tool, not a mission planner. The translations are machine-assisted and need native-speaker review. The project has not yet been tested with students, and the next step is a classroom trial to measure learning gain.
